title: School Virus Infection Simulator for Customizing School Schedules During COVID-19
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how schools can redesign schedules during COVID-19 to reduce in-school infection while preserving as much face-to-face instruction as possible. The authors argue that existing guidance, including UNESCO’s scheduling options, is too coarse to capture differences across school structures and classroom arrangements, especially self-contained versus departmentalized classrooms.

To address this, they developed the School-Virus-Infection-Simulator (SVIS), an agent-based infection simulator built on an extended susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed model and Wells-Riley airborne transmission equation. SVIS incorporates student schedules, classroom volume, ventilation, mask filtration assumptions, symptom timing, and the structure of lesson groups. The paper simulates several school schedule types, including UNESCO-style hybrid schedules and custom rotation patterns, under both self-contained and departmentalized classroom settings.

The context is K-12 schooling during the COVID-19 pandemic, with parameters chosen to represent classrooms and schedules in schools rather than a specific real school population. The simulation experiments examine one initial infected student over 12 weeks and compare outcomes such as maximum simultaneous infections and percentage of face-to-face lessons.

The main conclusion is that increasing classroom ventilation helps, but customizing schedules can be more stable and impactful. Infection outcomes depend strongly on the interaction between schedule design and classroom type, and some schedules with lower face-to-face percentages can perform better or worse than more in-person-heavy schedules depending on symptom timing and classroom organization. The authors conclude that SVIS can help teachers and education policymakers choose schedules that balance infection control with instructional continuity.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed simulation/modeling study, but it is not an empirical evaluation in schools and provides no randomized or quasi-experimental evidence on student outcomes. Credibility is limited to model assumptions and parameterization rather than observed K-12 implementation data.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful institutional decision-support benefits, but it reports no direct educational effect sizes and no observed implementation impact. Its findings are useful for planning, but the real-world impact on K-12 learning outcomes remains unclear.

interventions.use_case: agent-based school virus infection simulator (SVIS) for modeling how school schedules, classroom type, ventilation, and cohorting affect COVID-19 transmission in K-12 school settings

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that the SVIS can help teachers and education policymakers plan school schedules to reduce simultaneous infections while preserving face-to-face instruction. Across simulated scenarios, increasing ventilation reduced peak simultaneous infections, and schedule design materially changed infection risk depending on whether classrooms were self-contained or departmentalized.
finding.measure: Maximum number of students infected simultaneously; percentage of face-to-face lessons; simulated infection probability under different school schedules

finding.finding_summary: The simulator provides a decision-support tool for school administrators by comparing multiple scheduling options without physically implementing them. It is intended to help staff select schedules that balance infection control and instructional time, reducing uncertainty in operational planning.
finding.measure: Simulation-based schedule comparison utility for school policymakers
